topic.topic: How Gift Cards Make Money for Retailers

learningValue: Tests whether a primary-filing money-flow story with honest estimates holds attention on a consumer subject; a weak result with strong first-minute retention would point at the middle accounting sections.
selectedTitle: Billions Sit on Unused Gift Cards. Who Keeps the Money?
hookCandidates: In the US, Starbucks cards don't expire. Its latest annual report still counts $222.4 million of card money as sales, and no drink was served for it.
Look at the gift card in your kitchen drawer. The company that sold it has already estimated how likely you are to spend it.
When a gift card balance goes unspent, who ends up with the money?
Darden's gift cards have no expiry date. Its accountants still plan, 12 years ahead, for the money that won't come back.
A gift card is money the store owes you. Some of that debt slowly turns into the store's sales.
43% of American adults are holding an unused gift card, voucher or store credit, according to one survey. Here is where that money goes.

beats.text: In the US, Starbucks cards don't expire. Its latest annual report still counts $222.4 million of card money as sales, and no drink was served for it.
That money came from unused gift card balances.
The reason is a forecast. Starbucks keeps the share of card money that its own history says will never be spent, and it counts that share as sales.
That's only part of the story. Who else ends up with a piece of the money, and what can you still do about yours?
Start with the drawer. In August 2024, Bankrate paid the polling firm YouGov to ask 2,373 American adults about gift cards they hadn't used.
43% said they had at least one unused gift card, voucher or store credit.
The average holder was sitting on $244. The median was $100, which means half of the people with leftover value had $100 or less.

Bankrate turned that into a national figure of about $27 billion. Treat that as an estimate. It comes from an online survey, it counts vouchers and store credit too, and Bankrate doesn't publish the calculation behind the total.
Of the 2,373 people asked, 1,010 had some unused value. Everything after that is an estimate stretched across the whole country.
The same survey found that 34% of adults had already lost money to a gift card mistake. 20% let a card expire. 17% lost one. 12% watched the store close before they could spend it.
Now look at the other side of the counter. When you load money onto a card, the store gets the cash right away. But it can't call that cash sales, because it hasn't sold you anything yet.
Until you spend it, the money sits on the company's books as something it owes you. Accountants call it deferred revenue.
Starbucks keeps a small table for this in its annual report. Money goes in as card loads, reloads and loyalty rewards. In fiscal 2025, that added about $15.2 billion.
Money comes out of the same table as purchases and breakage. That side was also about $15.2 billion. So almost everything loaded in a year gets used. The interesting part is the slice that doesn't.

By the end of that year, Starbucks still owed customers about $1.75 billion, up from about $1.72 billion a year earlier. That figure mixes card balances with loyalty rewards, so it isn't a count of forgotten gift cards.
Starbucks has years of data on how people use its cards. From that history, it estimates how much of the money will not be redeemed.
Accountants have a name for that share. They call it breakage.
And the forecast isn't one number for the whole world. Starbucks says it builds its redemption rates market by market, using when each card was activated or reloaded, and through which channel.
Starbucks doesn't wait for a card to go quiet and then take the balance. It books breakage gradually, in step with the cards that do get spent.
Its filing puts the whole idea in one dry line. A portion of stored value cards is not expected to be redeemed.
Every time a regular customer taps a card at the register, a small predicted share of the unspent money moves into sales along with it.
Add up the two breakage lines in its filing and you get $222.4 million for fiscal 2025. That addition is ours. The year before, it was $207.6 million. The year before that, $215.0 million.
So money that customers never spend doesn't vanish. It shows up, a little at a time, as revenue the company never had to brew anything for.
Which raises an awkward question. If the cards don't expire, how does a company decide that any of the money is gone?
It makes a forecast. Darden, the company that runs Olive Garden, spells this out in its own annual report.
Its gift cards have no expiry date and no dormancy fees. It still estimates how much will never be used, and it spreads that money into sales over the expected life of the cards, generally 12 years.
Twelve years is the window over which Darden expects its remaining card balances to come in. Some of that money will be spent in the next decade. Some of it, the company predicts, never will.
It also admits the estimate could be off. Darden says moving its breakage rate by half a percentage point would have changed its breakage income by about $3.6 million in fiscal 2026.
And the pool of unspent cards isn't shrinking. In fiscal 2026, Darden took in $760.2 million on new cards.
It released $751.9 million through spending and breakage. By our math, the pile still grew by $7.9 million.
So breakage isn't a tally of cards people forgot. It's a bet, placed years in advance, on how a whole crowd of card holders will behave.
There's a reason companies plan this way instead of letting cards die. Federal rules make that hard.
A store gift card in the US can only carry an expiration date if its money stays good for at least five years from when it was issued or last loaded.
Fees for not using the card are allowed only after a full year with no activity, and then no more than one a month.
So the law doesn't let a store run out the clock on you quickly. What's left is the slow version. Wait, watch how people use their cards, and estimate.

That doesn't mean money never disappears. 20% of adults in the Bankrate survey said they'd let a card expire. That survey covered every kind of card and voucher, and some cards can still expire once the five-year minimum has passed.
There's also a third party with a claim. Starbucks says its breakage estimate takes into account money it may have to hand over to government agencies under unclaimed property laws.
The filing doesn't say how much goes where. It only confirms that part of an unspent balance can end up with the government instead of the company.

Darden is just as careful. It lists unclaimed property laws among the rules that are highly complex and that involve many subjective assumptions, estimates and judgments. Even the state's share is a judgment call.

It's tempting to put these numbers side by side. Don't. Bankrate's $27 billion is a survey estimate of what households say they hold, across every brand. Starbucks' $222.4 million is what one company recorded under accounting rules.
Breakage itself is an estimate too, and the companies say so. Darden updates its breakage rate from time to time. If people spend old cards more than history suggests, the numbers change.
So who keeps the money from an unspent gift card?

The store keeps a piece of the money, but only the share its own history says won't come back, and only a little at a time. And that's a forecast, not a transfer. The balance on your card is still yours to spend. The government may end up with another piece under unclaimed property laws.

At Starbucks and Darden, that balance has no expiry date. The forecast about you was made long before the card reached your drawer. If there's a card in there now, spending it is the only way to prove the forecast wrong.

authoring.winningHook: In the US, Starbucks cards don't expire. Its latest annual report still counts $222.4 million of card money as sales, and no drink was served for it.

storyPlan.thesis: An unused gift card balance is not simply lost money: issuers of cards that never expire predict from their own redemption history how much will never be spent, and book that share as revenue little by little as other cards are redeemed, while federal rules block the quickest ways of taking the balance from the holder.
storyPlan.centralQuestion: When a gift card balance goes unspent, who ends up with the money?

conflict.wants: Retailers want the cash up front and revenue they can count on; card holders want the value they were given.
conflict.obstacle: Accounting rules stop a store from calling the cash sales until something is sold, and federal rules stop it from simply expiring the card.
conflict.stakes: Survey estimates put tens of billions of dollars in American drawers; for one company the predicted leftovers were $222.4 million in a year.

storyPlan.misconception: That a store gets the money when a card is forgotten or expires, all at once.
storyPlan.originalAngle: Follow the money through the companies' own current filings (Starbucks fiscal 2025, Darden fiscal 2026): the card as a debt, breakage as a forecast spread over years, the federal floor, and the state's claim. Competitors covered the Delaware escheat angle (PolyMatter, 2023), market size and unspent totals (CNBC, 2020) and Starbucks' payments float (WSJ, 2022); none walks through how the predicted leftovers are booked or separates the survey estimate from what companies record.

storyPlan.payoff: The company keeps the share its own history says will not come back, recorded a little at a time; part may go to a state under unclaimed property laws; the rest still belongs to the holder, and at Starbucks and Darden it does not expire.
caveats: The $27 billion total is a survey estimate whose calculation is not published.
Breakage is a company estimate that is revised.
Starbucks' $1.75 billion balance mixes cards and loyalty rewards.
storyPlan.selectedHook: In the US, Starbucks cards don't expire. Its latest annual report still counts $222.4 million of card money as sales, and no drink was served for it.
storyPlan.selectionReason: Same contradiction as the heuristic winner, but built on Starbucks, a brand nearly every US viewer has used, and on the film's headline number; Darden is less familiar to a general audience and its 12-year detail pays off better mid-film.

problems.quote: The store keeps part of the money... The rest still belongs to the person holding the card.
problems.fix: Implies the predicted share stops being the holder's. It doesn't: Starbucks cards have no expiry and no fees that reduce balances, so breakage is an accounting forecast, not a transfer. Say the balance is still the holder's to spend. (Found in the final editorial read, after the automated checks passed.)

problems.quote: In its latest annual report, Starbucks counted $222.4 million...
problems.fix: Open with the approved contradiction hook: the cards don't expire, yet $222.4 million of card money became sales. The tension is in one line instead of two.

problems.quote: The answer runs through an accounting rule, a federal law, and a forecast...
problems.fix: By second 30 give the first real answer: the company predicted the unspent share from its own history and books it as sales. Keep 'who ends up with it' for the payoff. Cut the three-part teaser.

problems.quote: The company does, but only the share...
problems.fix: Answer the question in its own words ('the store keeps part of the money') so the payoff clearly closes the question opened in the first minute.

problems.quote: There's also a third party with a claim...
problems.fix: The section only restates one Starbucks line. Add Darden's own wording that unclaimed property laws involve subjective estimates and judgments: it shows the state's share is itself uncertain.

problems.quote: Darden took in $760.2 million on new cards and released $751.9 million...
problems.fix: Three numbers in one sentence. Split in, out and growth into separate sentences.

problems.quote: Almost all of it comes back out again, as drinks and food.
problems.fix: Show the evidence for 'almost all': the same filing table puts both money in and money out at about $15.2 billion. Name the table so the viewer sees it is the company's own record.
Say what a median means in plain words: half of the people with leftover value had $100 or less.
